attacks.claim: The PlugCloud signing scheme (header names, 'v1=' prefix, hex HMAC-SHA256 over '<timestamp>.<raw body>') is asserted but never grounded in vendor documentation or a vendor-produced test vector. The tests only round-trip the implementation's own sign() helper, so they cannot show compatibility. A mismatch would surface only as every delivery returning 401 after deploy.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no vendor doc link, captured real delivery, or known-good fixture. "PlugCloud signs every delivery with X-PC-Timestamp and X-PC-Signature: v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of \"<timestamp>.<raw body>\">" is stated as fact; test_signing.py's sign() reuses the same formula as the production code.

attacks.claim: Rejected deliveries are logged only at warning level with no metric or alert. A wrong or rotated secret would silently drop all readings until someone notices gaps in the data. There is also no documented key-rotation path (no dual-secret acceptance window).
attacks.evidence: log.warning("plugcloud webhook rejected: %s", exc)  ... raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="invalid signature")

attacks.claim: Enforcement is switched on unconditionally, with no shadow or log-only mode. A misconfigured secret makes the endpoint reject everything, and the vendor's retry behaviour during that window is not described.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no feature flag, log-only mode, or retry/backfill note. The route now raises 401 before any ingest for every unsigned or mismatched request.

attacks.claim: The PR description says the endpoint returns a bare 401, but the code returns a JSON detail body. This is a spec mismatch, though not a security leak since the detail string is fixed.
attacks.evidence: "returns a bare 401 on any failure" vs "raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail=\"invalid signature\") from None"

attacks.claim: The signature comparison is case-sensitive and assumes lowercase hex. If the vendor emits uppercase hex, or any other encoding variant, valid deliveries are rejected. The verifier also accepts a signature without the 'v1=' prefix and does not reject unknown versions.
attacks.evidence: expected = hmac.new(...).hexdigest() ... signature.removeprefix("v1=").encode()

attacks.claim: There is no nonce or delivery-ID dedup, so a captured valid delivery can be replayed for 5 minutes. The upsert is idempotent for identical data, but a replay can revert a reading that was later corrected for the same (device_id, measured_at).
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: replay protection. Tolerance check only: if abs(current - int(timestamp)) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS: raise SignatureError(...)

attacks.claim: The secret validator checks only length. Low-entropy values such as 32 repeated characters pass startup.
attacks.evidence: if len(v.get_secret_value()) < 32: raise ValueError("must be at least 32 characters")

attacks.claim: The body is read fully into memory with no cap in the application. Safety relies entirely on an external reverse-proxy limit that is not enforced or tested in this repo. Before this change the body was also read in full, so this is not a regression, but it is an unverified dependency.
attacks.evidence: body = await request.body()  (context only: "the reverse proxy caps request bodies at 1 MB")

attacks.claim: Existing tests that POST unsigned payloads to /webhooks/plugcloud would now fail with 401, and the PR does not show them being updated. Docs, .env.example, and compose files are also not updated for the new required VOLTLOG_PLUGCLOUD_SECRET.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: changes to existing webhook route tests, .env.example, or docker-compose. Diff only touches tests/conftest.py and adds tests/webhooks/test_signing.py.

attacks.claim: The secret check only enforces length, so a 32-character low-entropy value passes startup. The reverse proxy is the only bound on body size, because the handler reads the full body before any check.
attacks.evidence: if len(v.get_secret_value()) < 32: raise ValueError("must be at least 32 characters")

attacks.claim: No attack. The change adds no new personal data collection, retention, or exposure. The warning log records only the exception text, not the body or secret.
attacks.evidence: log.warning("plugcloud webhook rejected: %s", exc)

attacks.claim: No attack. The change is self-contained, adds no vendor dependency beyond the existing PlugCloud webhook, and keeps the instance self-hostable.
attacks.evidence: signing.py uses only hashlib, hmac, re, and time from the standard library

attacks.claim: The get_db dependency is resolved before signature verification, so unauthenticated requests still open database resources. Each rejected request also writes a log line, which allows log flooding.
attacks.evidence: async def plugcloud_webhook(request: Request, db: Database = Depends(get_db), settings: Settings = Depends(get_settings))

attacks.claim: No attack. The change adds no paid API or token spend. Compute per request is one HMAC over at most the proxy-capped body.
attacks.evidence: hmac.new(secret, timestamp.encode() + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256)

attacks.claim: A legitimate delivery retried more than 5 minutes after its original timestamp gets a permanent 401. If PlugCloud retries with the original timestamp during an outage, those readings are rejected and may be lost. The artifact does not establish the vendor's retry or re-stamping behavior.
attacks.evidence: rejects deliveries more than 5 minutes old or in the future, and returns a bare 401 on any failure

attacks.claim: Deploying this makes a new secret mandatory and changes the endpoint from open to authenticated. Vendor and operator must coordinate the secret. The design has no rotation path, since only one secret is accepted.
attacks.evidence: plugcloud_secret: SecretStr (required, no rotation or secondary-key field)

attacks.claim: The 422 response changes the error body format from FastAPI's default. Signature hex is compared case-sensitively, and multi-signature headers are not handled. Both may fail for valid vendor deliveries if the vendor sends them.
attacks.evidence: raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail="invalid payload") from None

attacks.claim: The claim that startup fails when the secret is missing or short is untested and unverified. get_settings is not shown and may be evaluated lazily on the first request. The PlugCloud retry behavior assumed by the 5-minute window is not cited.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no startup test and no get_settings implementation; the test suite constructs Settings directly

attacks.claim: No attack. The change has no rendered UI surface.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no UI files in the diff

attacks.claim: No attack. The change solves the stated spoofing problem, which is real, for the owner of the instance.
attacks.evidence: anyone who found the URL could inject fake readings

attacks.claim: No attack. Verification adds no user-facing steps beyond the operator setting one env var.
attacks.evidence: New required env vars are announced in release notes and set by the operator in the compose .env file

attacks.claim: No attack. The change has no interface that affects accessibility.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no UI or copy changes in the diff

attacks.claim: No attack. The change adds no regulated data processing or licensing issue.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no compliance-relevant content in the artifact

attacks.claim: The conftest change requires every test that builds Settings to pass a secret, which is hidden coupling. Other Settings constructions outside the shown diff may fail.
attacks.evidence: return Settings(database_url=TEST_DB_URL, plugcloud_secret="t" * 32)

attacks.claim: Within the 5-minute window a captured valid delivery can be replayed. The upsert keyed on (device_id, measured_at) makes this idempotent, so it is not gate-worthy, but replay protection is not claimed.
attacks.evidence: abs(current - int(timestamp)) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS, with no nonce or seen-set
